transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-07-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (CTO - Aurora), Ethan Morales (Lead ML Eng), Sara Patel (SRE)

Summary: quick integration discovery focused on SDKs and orchestration patterns; customer leaning toward a Dedicated or Private option for compliance but wants to validate integration path with LangChain / LlamaIndex and gateway/proxy approach. Discussed quotas, observability hooks, and preferred telemetry.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, I'll kick things off. Are we all good on time?
[00:08] Priya: Yep, good here. Thanks.
[00:12] Liam: Hi all, Liam on the SE side. We'll go over integration options and some patterns other customers use.
[00:18] Ethan: Hi, Ethan. We mostly want to understand the SDK story, how you fit into our langchain pipeline and gtw proxy architecture.
[00:25] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: SDKs (Python/Node), LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy pattern and network topology for Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, rate limits/quotas and token billing, and observability hooks (console, traces, Prometheus). Then Q&A and next steps.

[01:02] Liam: To start, our SDKs are lightweight - Python and Node. They wrap the REST API and support streaming, function calls and structured outputs. We also maintain official LangChain connectors and a maintained LlamaIndex adapter; examples in the repo.
[01:18] Ethan: Sorry, are those first-party adapters or community-contrib? We use LangChain heavily and need stable adapters for production.
[01:26] Liam: Good question. The LangChain connector is first-party, we publish examples and tests. LlamaIndex adapter is maintained too, but there are a few community-backed helpers — we keep a compatibility matrix in the docs.
[01:40] Priya: How does auth look in the SDK? We run requests through an internal gateway/proxy that injects headers and does token rotation.
[01:48] Liam: You can do API keys or mTLS for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted you typically use API keys stored in a secrets manager behind your proxy. SDKs support passing a bearer token or a short-lived token. We also have support for proxying to the Redwood gateway - basically you can direct SDK traffic to a local gateway endpoint that proxies to Redwood and injects your internal auth.
[02:12] Sara: That proxy pattern - is it just a pass-through or do you recommend adding a local rate-limit layer?
[02:18] Liam: Customers commonly do both. We recommend per-route quotas upstream and then local token-bucket limits at the proxy to protect internal backends. Redwood has configurable quotas at the API key and org level: calls-per-second and tokens-per-minute.
[02:32] Ethan: Tokens-per-minute is new to me — is billing also token-based?
[02:36] Maya: Yes, billing is token-based for the Hosted API. For Dedicated we do a reserved capacity model plus overage token billing if you choose it. Private is typically a license + infra cost.

[03:05] [crosstalk] Priya: Our compliance team insists on private networking — VPC peering or an on-prem option. What are the tradeoffs?
[03:12] Liam: With Redwood Dedicated you get a customer-isolated GPU pool that can live in a dedicated VPC and we support VPC peering. For Private deployments we can do an on-prem bundle or private control plane with customer-managed network. The tightest control is Private (air-gapped if needed) but it adds lead time. Dedicated hits a balance — still our runtime but provisioned for you.
[03:38] Priya: And SOC2 / ISO?
[03:41] Maya: We'll share SOC2 and ISO artifacts. Dedicated and Hosted are SOC2 compliant; Private customers can manage their own audit controls and we support submitting logs to your SIEM.

[04:10] Ethan: Back to the SDK->LangChain flow: we have a pipeline where LangChain agents call into a medium-sized model for embeddings and a larger model for generation. Anyone used Redwood for that pattern?
[04:22] Liam: Yep - common. For embeddings we have efficient endpoints and batching. For generation you can configure model variants and pin versions. The SDK includes a batch API and automatic prefix caching (KV cache) for chat sessions — that reduces token cost.
[04:36] Ethan: Did you say K-V cash? (laughs) Sorry, K-V cache.
[04:40] Liam: (laughs) K-V cache. It's an in-memory store to speed up continuing conversations.

[05:05] Priya: Observability — we need traceability per request and cost breakdown. What hooks do you expose?
[05:12] Liam: We emit request-level telemetry: trace IDs, request latency, tokens in/out, per-route cost estimates. Those can be streamed to a customer webhook, pushed into a Prometheus metrics gateway, or consumed in the Redwood Console. We also have per-token cost breakdowns in the billing API.
[05:30] Sara: Do you provide OpenTelemetry spans or is it custom?
[05:34] Liam: We support both. Out of the box you'll get our trace headers (x-rd-trace-id) and you can correlate in your tracing system. For Dedicated/Private we can integrate with your OTLP endpoint.

[06:02] Maya: A common pattern is to run a small gateway in front of LangChain that adds instrumentation and per-customer routing then forwards to Redwood. That lets you swap model backends if needed.
[06:14] Ethan: That matches our plan. How do you handle retries and timeouts? LangChain has its own retry logic.
[06:20] Liam: We recommend neat layering: set conservative timeouts at the proxy (e.g., 10s for generation depending on model) and let the SDK surface streaming partials. Redwood's client supports chunked streaming so you can show progressive tokens while LangChain orchestration continues. Retries should be idempotent where possible and you can use trace IDs to dedupe.

[07:00] Priya: Performance — we target p95 < 300ms for small prompts and the rest under 1s. Can Redwood meet that on Hosted?
[07:09] Maya: For small models and short context windows Hosted can meet those latencies in many regions. If you require strict p95 targets we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity and fine-tuned autoscaling. Also quantized variants can reduce latency.
[07:26] Ethan: Speaking of quantization, do you provide quantized kernels and recommendations?
[07:29] Liam: Yes, we publish recommended quant profiles per model and workload. For inference you can choose int8 or int4 where acceptable. We'll run evals on your prompt sets in a PoC to recommend settings.

[08:00] Maya: Let's talk quotas — what's realistic to expect?
[08:05] Liam: For Hosted we put soft quotas and rate-limits on a per-key basis, e.g. 60 requests/min and a tokens-per-minute cap; those are configurable through support for larger customers. Dedicated gives much higher per-key throughput and you can set per-route limits. Private you fully control.
[08:24] Priya: We need burst protection — spikes during peak product events. Can Redwood do autoscale bursts?
[08:30] Liam: Dedicated has burst pools and autoscale policies; we can provision burst capacity for predictable events. For Hosted we have regional auto-burst but less guaranteed.

[09:05] Ethan: Integration detail — is there a workshop or example repo for LangChain + Redwood + local gateway?
[09:10] Liam: We have a repo with example patterns: a small gateway (Node), LangChain agent config, and a sample LlamaIndex connector. We'll include a sample docker-compose to run locally.
[09:20] Priya: Can you show us how secrets are rotated when using a proxy?
[09:24] Liam: Sure — typical flow: the proxy retrieves secrets from your vault and issues short-lived tokens to downstream services. The SDK supports token refresh hooks so you don't need to restart processes. We'll include snippet in the guide.

[10:00] Priya: Any gotchas?
[10:04] Liam: A couple: keep an eye on effective token counts when you do chain-of-thought style prompts; LangChain can accumulate tokens across steps. Also, when using caching, ensure prompt canonicalization so cache hits are reliable. Finally, watch concurrency for KV cache size — that's why we suggest measured staging runs.

[10:40] Ethan: How do you handle changelogs and model rollouts? We need predictable rollouts and quick rollback.
[10:46] Maya: We support rollouts and can pin model versions. Console gives canary/A-B options and an automatic fallback to a stable variant if latency or errors cross thresholds.

[11:15] Priya: Security: SAML/SSO for the console and RBAC for teams?
[11:19] Maya: Yes — SSO via SAML/OIDC, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC with fine-grained roles. For Private you can plug in your identity provider.

[12:02] Ethan: Cost control — is there proactive alerting when cost or unusual token usage happens?
[12:08] Liam: Yes, you can set spend caps, alerts on token usage spikes, and route-level cost estimation in Console. We also recommend using batching and prefix caching to reduce unit costs.

[12:40] Priya: Okay, last bit — observability demo? Do you have a quick screenshot or link?
[12:46] Maya: We'll send a short console video and example dashboards.

Wrap / Recap:
[13:00] Maya: Recap: we will share sandbox API keys and the LangChain/LlamaIndex example repo, Liam will prepare quant and batching recommendations based on the 512-token median workload, Priya will share traffic profile and SLOs. We'll schedule a follow-up SE PoC planning session.
